description:
Parallel agent worktrees each build into their own target directory, so build artifacts on a development host grow with the number of worktrees rather than with the size of the workspace.

## Background

Agent work happens in git worktrees under the repository, each carrying its own Cargo target directory. Dependency artifacts dominate those directories and are identical across worktrees of one workspace, so every additional worktree duplicates several gigabytes that differ only in the crate being edited.

Observed on a development host: thirty-nine worktrees held roughly 170 GB of build artifacts, most belonging to worktrees whose work had merged waves earlier. The root filesystem reached zero available bytes mid-build. The two build steps that need multi-gigabyte scratch space then failed with empty diagnostic files, which reads as a flaky check rather than an exhausted disk, so the real cause cost a full diagnostic cycle to find.

Two existing properties make one shared location viable. Cargo already serializes concurrent builds against a single target directory under its own lock, and the heaviest build step already serializes on a host-wide lock, so most of the added contention is already paid. The build-footprint budget derives its executable measurements from Cargo's own output rather than by scanning the target directory, so sharing that directory across worktrees does not inflate the measured footprint.

Holding build artifacts in memory instead was rejected: the workspace's artifacts exceed the memory available on a development host, which converts an exhausted disk into an exhausted address space, and the failure is harder to read.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Builds started from any worktree of the repository write their artifacts to one shared location rather than one location per worktree.
- [hard] REQ-02: The build-footprint budget check reports the same measurements under the shared location as under a per-worktree one, and the incremental-state check applies to it unchanged.
- [hard] REQ-03: Deleting a worktree leaves the shared artifacts intact and usable by the remaining worktrees.
- [hard] REQ-04: Two builds started concurrently from different worktrees both complete, and neither observes a partially written artifact.
- [hard] REQ-05: Contributor documentation states where build artifacts live and how to reclaim them, including artifacts belonging to worktrees whose work has already merged.

## Notes

Artifacts belong on a disk-backed path. A memory-backed filesystem is exhausted by a workspace build on a host of ordinary size.

## Resolution

Rejected 2026-08-14: the reported disk pressure is real, but this remedy is the
wrong one for it.

Measured on the development host at rejection time: 23 agent worktrees holding
92 GB, 17 of them carrying a private target directory, with the root filesystem
at 92% used. Sixteen of those worktrees were fully merged into main. The
dominant cost is worktree lifetime, not artifact duplication across live
worktrees: removing the merged checkouts reclaimed most of the 92 GB at no
throughput cost, while sharing one target directory would serialize every
concurrent agent build against Cargo's single target lock and charge the whole
fleet wall-clock for a saving that worktree removal already delivers.

The incremental-state objection previously recorded against a shared target
directory no longer applies — `jit:0708d692` made the incremental policy judge
what a gate run itself produced rather than ambient state — so this rejection
rests on the throughput trade-off, not on that blocker.
title: Share one Cargo target directory across agent worktrees
